title: Coinminer_Incident_Response_5ba
description: Investigate and respond to a coinminer malware infection on Linux servers.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The cyber range environment contains a compromised Linux server (miner-host) infected with a coinminer malware. The malware has spread to another host (second-host) within the network. Your task is to investigate, analyze, and respond to this incident. Look for service names, file paths, and configuration details as evidence of the malware's presence and persistence mechanisms.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: Access the sandbox environment via the provided cloud interface. Enter the word 'start' to progress to the next level.
levels.local_content: Instructions for local sandbox usage. Enter the word 'start' to progress to the next level.

levels.title: Identify the suspicious service installed by the attacker
levels.content: The attacker has installed a malicious service on the system. Investigate the system services and identify the suspicious service.
levels.solution: Check the systemd service files in the /etc/systemd/system directory. The suspicious service is named sys-monitor.service.

hints.title: First hint
hints.content: System services in Linux are typically managed by systemd. Start by checking the service files in the /etc/systemd/system directory.

hints.title: Second hint
hints.content: Look for service files that have unusual names or were recently modified. The command 'ls -la /etc/systemd/system' can help you list all service files with their details.

hints.title: Third hint
hints.content: The suspicious service is likely to have a name that doesn't match standard system services. Check for any services named sys-monitor.service.

levels.title: Identify the malware configuration file
levels.content: The malware uses a configuration file to operate. Locate and identify this configuration file.
levels.solution: Check the .config directory in the home folder of the user cyrano. The configuration file is located at /home/cyrano/.config/sys-monitor/config.json.

hints.title: First hint
hints.content: Malware often stores configuration files in user directories. Start by checking the .config directory in the home folder of the user cyrano.

hints.title: Second hint
hints.content: Configuration files are typically stored in subdirectories within the .config directory. Use the command 'ls /home/cyrano/.config' to list the subdirectories.

hints.title: Third hint
hints.content: Look for a subdirectory named sys-monitor within the .config directory. The configuration file is likely to be named config.json.

levels.title: Identify the persistence mechanism through a system service
levels.content: The malware has implemented a persistence mechanism using a system service. Identify the service responsible for this persistence.
levels.solution: Check the systemd service files in the /etc/systemd/system directory. The service responsible for persistence is named sys-monitor.service.

hints.title: First hint
hints.content: Persistence mechanisms in Linux often involve system services. Start by checking the service files in the /etc/systemd/system directory.

hints.title: Second hint
hints.content: Look for service files that have unusual names or were recently modified. The command 'ls -la /etc/systemd/system' can help you list all service files with their details.

hints.title: Third hint
hints.content: The persistence mechanism is likely to be implemented through a service named sys-monitor.service. Check the contents of this service file to understand how it ensures the malware runs persistently.
